question: Does a retained skill library make each later skill cheaper, and does the discount grow with the library?
answer: The first is true exactly once. Going from one skill to two makes the next skill dramatically cheaper in both task families; going from two to three or three to four confers nothing measurable. Transfer is a first-composition effect and does not compound.
regime: All cells measured on rectified (exact-zero) slot gates with a 5% gate warmup, so per-rung interference is at zero and no advantage can be a borrowing artifact.

estimator.primary: pooled paired accuracy difference across the budget grid, deep arm minus shallow arm, paired within seed, with an exact sign test
estimator.secondary: interpolated experience to a fixed accuracy target, paired within seed
estimator.note: The two disagree at ancestry 1->2 on the hidden-rule task because the deep arm's advantage is concentrated mid-curve and the curves reconverge at threshold. A threshold ratio samples one point; the pooled delta uses the whole curve and has far more power.

depth_not_family.statement: Ancestry depth and task family were confounded in earlier work: the rung that transferred was visible and zero-shot, the rungs that did not were hidden-rule and few-shot. A hidden-rule task at ancestry 1->2 transfers at +0.0648 (p=7.3e-9) while the same family at 2->3 and 3->4 gives -0.0163 and -0.0002. The effect is set by depth.
depth_not_family.family_extensibility: The gate suite needs the audited reversal to flip at least 80% of actions. In the visible family correct = f(identity, context) only XOR-type f qualifies, and those are exhausted: and/or flip 50%. In the hidden-rule family correct = rule ^ f(identity, context), reversing the rule flips every action for any f, so that family extends indefinitely.

retires: The earlier reading that the advantage shrank across rungs (1.231 -> 1.083) with interference as the binding constraint. Removing interference did not restore compounding; there was never a compounding curve, only a first-composition effect measured twice at different depths.

new_primitives.properties: no aliasing against any existing task, rule reversal flips 100% of actions with pixel-identical rendering, marginal action balanced

cue_capacity_limit.observation: Placing the two new cue slots required a preflight separability search. Bottom-band candidates scored 0.22-0.58 against the two cues already there, below the interference threshold; top-band candidates reached 1.01-1.09 regardless of area or intensity.
cue_capacity_limit.cause: The encoder's closing global average pool. Position band dominates separability; area and intensity are weak secondary axes.
cue_capacity_limit.consequence: The frozen encoder can only tell so many operations apart and that budget is nearly spent. Further extension needs a cue code the pooled encoder can resolve, or an encoder retaining spatial detail.

method_notes: 0 dead slots in the 112-run rung-4 race and 0 in the 576-run rung-3 sweep, confirming the gate warmup at scale. Two dead slots appear in the smallest-budget cells of the 1->2 hidden sweep, where 5% of 24 updates rounds to one warmup update.
The original 1->2 hidden grid and the 3->4 grid saturate above 512 updates; the unsaturated figures are reported alongside.
Each depth necessarily uses a different new task, since a skill cannot be learned twice. The family control addresses the largest version of that confound but not all of it.
claim_boundary: Four ancestry depths, two task families, one architecture, 8 to 16 seeds per cell. This bounds where transfer lives in this ladder; it is not a general claim about continual learning.
